newsitem.title: USA: Hartford Life's IPO seen ensured for success.
newsitem.headline: Hartford Life's IPO seen ensured for success.

text.p: Hartford Life Inc's solid business prospects, sound results and established name should ensure a very respectable debut for the Hartford Financial Services Group Inc unit's initial public offering, despite some concerns about the deal's valuation.
The 23 million share offering is expected to price within a range of $24 to $27 a share.

"This price is not cheap," said Nutmeg Securities analyst Ira Zuckerman. "But my guess is the stock will probably go to a premium anyway because it's an attractive area of the life insurance industry -- the growing area of annuities, especially variable." Annuities form the backbone of Hartford Life's business, and net income from this segment has grown to $145 million in 1996 from $35 million in 1992.

Based on 1996 sales, the company is the largest writer of individual annuities in the United States. In that year, it sold $9.8 billion of individual annuities, of which $9.3 billion were individual variable annuities.

An annuity is a contract that provides a periodic income at regular intervals. With a variable annuity, the amount may fluctuate in relation to securities market values or the value of other underlying investments.

Ryan Jacob, director of research at IPO Value Monitor, said that though Hartford Life probably deserved to trade at something of a premium in relation to its peers, the pricing seemed a tad high. "It's one of the highest quality insurance companies probably out there...however, in our minds it's a little too rich," he said.

He said that many companies falling within the peer group, which include Nationwide Financial Services Inc, Torchmark Corp, Protective Life Corp, and ReliaStar Financial Corp, trade at 12 to 16 times earnings.

"This one (Hartford Life), could trade over 20 times our expected 1997 earnings," said Jacob. He declined to say what his estimates were but said he sees Hartford's stock starting to trade at over $30 a share.
Vincent Slavin, who tracks IPOs for Cantor Fitzgerald, said he sees an opening premium of $2 to $3 on the deal.
The IPO will hold appeal for many investors because "it falls into so many people's universes," said Steve Zenker, portfolio manager at McCabe Capital Managers.

He said an issue like this represented a fairly safe investment, buttressed by the surety of a dividend yield. Hartford Life anticipates paying dividends, and sees an initial quarterly payout of $0.09 per share in the third quarter of 1997, according to its filing.
This translates into an annual yield of about 1.33 percent if a $27 share price were assumed. Not a fat payout, said Zenker, but a decent one by IPO standards.

Hartford Life earned $24 million in 1996 on total revenues of $4.4 billion, compared with $150 million in 1995 on revenues of $4.1 billion. The 1996 income included a loss of $225 million in the Guaranteed Investment Contracts segment.

The company said in its filing that it has pulled out of most of the general account guaranteed rate contract business, and as such, does not expect any material income or loss from the Guaranteed Investment Contract segment after 1996.

After the offering, Hartford Financial will still own 100 percent of Hartford Life's Class B stock, which translates into a stake of about 81.4 percent, assuming the underwriters' overallotment option were exercised in full.
Hartford Life is set to price late on Wednesday for trading on Thursday, according to lead underwriter Goldman Sachs. The stock is to trade on the New York Stock Exchange under the symbol HLI.N.
Of the total 23 million shares, 18.4 million are slated for the United States and 4.6 million are being offered in a concurrent international offering.
